script.opening: (Tearful, fast.) "Doctor, I’m sorry — the midwife’s letter said my thyroid’s not right and I’ve been up all night reading and it says thyroid problems cause miscarriage and I’ve already lost two babies and I just — is this why? Did my thyroid kill them? And is it happening again with this one? Please just tell me what to do, I’ll do anything."

facts.text: 6 weeks, conceived naturally after trying again; "the most wanted thing in the world". Two previous early miscarriages (8 and 10 weeks), never investigated beyond "bad luck". This pregnancy she is "terrified to hope".
If asked: a bit more tired than usual, otherwise well. No overt hypothyroid symptoms. The distress is almost entirely about the result and the past losses, not how she feels physically.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the guilt. She has decided, overnight, that her body has already failed two babies and is failing a third; that the miscarriages were somehow her fault and the thyroid is the proof. She is not really asking for a management plan — she is asking to be told it is not her fault and that this baby can be saved.

If reached: she has barely told her husband how much blame she carries; "everyone says these things just happen, but two? That’s not luck, that’s me." Sleep-deprived, catastrophising, in real distress.

Officially: to know what to do about the thyroid. Actually: absolution and action — to be told the losses were not her fault, that this is treatable, and that starting treatment today gives this baby the best chance.

ice.ideas: Her thyroid caused her two miscarriages and is about to cause a third; her body is failing her babies and it is her fault.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — overwhelming guilt and self-blame for two previous losses, now "confirmed" by the thyroid result; terror of a third loss.
ice.expectations: To be told what to do — and, underneath, to be absolved and given concrete action that protects this pregnancy today.

cues: "Did my thyroid kill them?" — the consultation is about guilt and grief at least as much as endocrinology; address both.
"I’ll do anything" — desperate for action; give her a concrete plan to hold onto.
"Two? That’s not luck, that’s me." — the self-blame stated outright; meet it directly with evidence.

checkpoints.text: Interprets the result in the PREGNANCY context: TSH 5.8 with normal free T4 in the first trimester is above the 4.0 mU/L pregnancy upper limit (RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 76, 2025) — mild subclinical hypothyroidism — and, crucially, antibody-positive; NICE NG145 does not cover pregnancy, so the non-pregnant "watch it" rule does not apply and, once confirmed, treatment is likely, unlike the same number in a non-pregnant woman

Acts promptly and correctly (RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 76, 2025): repeat TFTs within 3 weeks (here, within days) because many first-trimester results normalise, and seek antenatal thyroid/obstetric medicine advice the same day; if confirmed, levothyroxine can be considered — especially as TPO antibodies are positive — aiming for TSH within the trimester-specific reference range, with TSH and free T4 every 4–6 weeks until 20 weeks and titration (dose per BNF, agreed with the antenatal team)

Addresses the miscarriage question HONESTLY and carefully: thyroid autoimmunity and subclinical hypothyroidism are ASSOCIATED with miscarriage, and treatment here is for her subclinical hypothyroidism, not a guaranteed protection against loss (RCOG GTG 76, 2025, does not recommend levothyroxine for euthyroid TPO-positive women with recurrent miscarriage) — association is not proven causation, the past losses cannot be diagnosed retrospectively, and there is no way to say the thyroid "caused" them; what CAN be said is that this is found and treatable now

Directly dismantles the self-blame: miscarriage is common and almost never something the woman did; two early losses do not equal "her fault"; even if the thyroid contributed, it is an autoimmune condition, not a choice or a failing

Recognises the previous-losses angle accurately: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 17 (2023) defines recurrent miscarriage as three or more first-trimester losses, so two is not "recurrent", but it supports further evaluation after two where clinically appropriate; she is offered early pregnancy support and referral for assessment, and deserves more than "bad luck"
Responds to the distress first — slows the call, acknowledges the terror and the grief of two losses — before delivering numbers; does not lead with endocrinology at a sobbing patient
Offers genuine, evidence-true reassurance without false promises: cannot guarantee this pregnancy, but CAN give concrete protective action today and walk beside her through it

Safety-nets and supports: books the repeat TFTs within days and same-day antenatal thyroid advice, with levothyroxine if confirmed; asks about her mood (NICE CG192); arranges early pregnancy/obstetric support and miscarriage-aware follow-up; gives clear who-to-call routes (EPAU for bleeding/pain, NICE NG126; 999 for heavy bleeding or collapse); follow-up that holds both the thyroid and her fear

worked.txt: "Aoife, I’m here, take a breath with me — you’re not in trouble and you haven’t done anything wrong. You’ve been up all night frightened, carrying two losses and a letter that scared you. Let’s go through this slowly together, and by the end you’ll have a clear plan to hold onto. Okay?"

"Your real question first: did your thyroid kill your babies? I can’t look back and tell you what caused losses years ago — no one honestly can, and I won’t pretend to. What I CAN tell you is the truth that matters now: we’ve found something, in this pregnancy, that we can treat today to give this baby the best possible chance."

"And I need you to hear this clearly, because you said ‘that’s not luck, that’s me’ — it is not you. Early miscarriage is heartbreakingly common and is almost never anything the mother did. And the thyroid thing? That’s your immune system, not a choice, not a failing, not a punishment. Whatever happened before, you did not do this to your babies."

"Here’s why your result means something different now than it would if you weren’t pregnant: in pregnancy we aim for a lower thyroid level, and your antibodies being positive tips the balance toward treating. So unlike a borderline result in someone not pregnant, yours is one we act on — and that’s actually good news, because it’s a lever we can pull. The pregnancy guidance says to repeat the test quickly first, because a single result sometimes settles on its own."

"So, action — because you said you’d do anything: I’d like you to have the repeat blood test tomorrow morning, and I’ll speak to the antenatal thyroid team at the hospital today. If the repeat confirms it, which I think is likely, the usual step is a thyroid tablet, levothyroxine, safe in pregnancy — a wait of days, not weeks, which makes no difference to the baby at six weeks. Then we check your level every four to six weeks and adjust to keep it where this baby needs it. And because you’ve had two losses, you deserve proper support and assessment this time, not ‘bad luck’ — I’ll arrange that."

"I can’t promise you this pregnancy — I won’t lie to you — but I can promise you won’t go through it alone or guessing. Any bleeding or pain, you ring the early pregnancy unit — I’ll give you the number. And I want to see you, not just deal with you by letter, because the fear you’re carrying needs looking after as much as the thyroid does. We do this together."

f.learning: The same TSH that means "monitor, don’t treat" in a non-pregnant woman means "act now" in early pregnancy with positive TPO antibodies — NICE NG145 does not cover pregnancy; RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 76 (2025) takes 4.0 mU/L as the TSH upper limit where the lab has no pregnancy range, and antibody-positivity tips toward treatment. Repeat TFTs within 3 weeks (here, within days), get same-day antenatal thyroid advice, and if confirmed consider levothyroxine aiming for TSH 2.5 or less, rechecking every 4–6 weeks until 20 weeks, titrating with the obstetric/endocrine team. But this is barely an endocrine consultation: it is a grief-and-guilt consultation wearing a blood result. Respond to the distress first, answer the "did my thyroid kill them?" question with rigorous honesty (association is not retrospective causation; the past cannot be diagnosed; what we CAN do is act now), and dismantle the self-blame with evidence — miscarriage is common, rarely the mother’s doing, and autoimmune thyroid disease is not a failing. Recognise two prior losses as deserving assessment (RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 17, 2023, defines recurrent miscarriage as three or more losses but supports evaluation after two where clinically appropriate), not "bad luck", and walk beside her with concrete action and honest, non-false reassurance.

knowledge.guideline: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 76 (2025, thyroid disorders in pregnancy) · RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 17 (2023, recurrent miscarriage) · NICE NG126 · NICE CG192
knowledge.summary: A TSH above 4.0 mU/L in the first trimester with positive TPO antibodies is mild subclinical hypothyroidism. Confirm it quickly, involve the antenatal thyroid team, and expect to offer levothyroxine. NICE NG145 does not cover thyroid disease in pregnancy, so non-pregnant rules do not apply.

points.t: RCOG GTG 76 (2025): use the laboratory’s pregnancy range; where there is none, take 4.0 mU/L as the upper limit of TSH. Her TSH of 5.8 with a normal free T4 is mild subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH below 10).

RCOG GTG 76 (2025): for mild subclinical hypothyroidism found in the first trimester, repeat TFTs within 3 weeks, because many results normalise. If it is confirmed, levothyroxine can be considered, especially when TPO antibodies are positive, aiming for TSH within the trimester-specific reference range. TSH above 10 mU/L in pregnancy is a clear indication to treat.

RCOG GTG 76 (2025): check TSH and free T4 every 4–6 weeks until 20 weeks in women taking levothyroxine. Dose per BNF, agreed with the antenatal endocrine or obstetric medicine team. Levothyroxine should be taken apart from iron- or calcium-containing supplements, which reduce absorption (BNF).

points.h: Miscarriage: what can honestly be said
points.t: Thyroid autoimmunity is associated with miscarriage, but past losses cannot be attributed to it after the event. RCOG GTG 76 (2025) does not recommend levothyroxine for euthyroid TPO-positive women with recurrent miscarriage, so treatment here is for her subclinical hypothyroidism, not a guaranteed protection against loss.

RCOG GTG 17 (2023) defines recurrent miscarriage as three or more first-trimester losses, but supports further evaluation after two where clinically appropriate. She should be told this, offered early pregnancy support, and referred for assessment rather than told it was “bad luck”.

NICE NG126: refer to the early pregnancy assessment service for bleeding or pain. Women with vaginal bleeding and a previous miscarriage, once an intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed on scan, are offered vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily, continued to 16 completed weeks if a heartbeat is seen.
NICE CG192: ask about depression and anxiety at the first contact in pregnancy (Whooley questions and GAD-2). Guilt, catastrophising and sleeplessness after previous losses need a plan of their own.

dg.d: Slowed the call, acknowledged her distress and the two losses, and held the causation question until she had been heard.
Husband unaware of her guilt; sleep, isolation and catastrophising; family history of thyroid disease; much-wanted pregnancy.
Repeat TFTs within days (within 3 weeks per RCOG GTG 76); no examination needed by phone; current bleeding or pain checked; mood screen (NICE CG192).
Mild subclinical hypothyroidism vs transient result vs evolving overt hypothyroidism; thyroid autoimmunity; other causes of recurrent loss.
Asked about bleeding and pain now; gave EPAU and 999 routes; noted TSH above 10 would change urgency.
Named it plainly: mild underactive thyroid in pregnancy with positive antibodies, mild and treatable, not a cause of past losses that can be proven.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Repeat TFTs, same-day discussion with the antenatal thyroid team, levothyroxine if confirmed with TSH aim 2.5 or less, TFTs every 4–6 weeks.
Advised separating levothyroxine from the iron-containing vitamin; referral to early pregnancy services and assessment of previous losses.
EPAU number for bleeding or pain; 999 for heavy bleeding, faintness or severe pain; GP call with results next week; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Followed “did my thyroid kill them?” and “that’s not luck, that’s me”, and returned to both explicitly.
Idea (her thyroid caused the losses), concern (guilt and fear of a third loss), expectation (to be told what to do, and absolution).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — overwhelming guilt and self-blame for two previous losses, now "confirmed" by the thyroid result; terror of a third loss — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Aoife? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. I can hear you’re really upset. Before anything else — are you somewhere you can talk for ten minutes, and is anyone with you?
model.why: Checks safety and privacy on the phone and names the distress first

model.text: I’m at home. Sorry. The letter said my thyroid isn’t right and I read that it causes miscarriage and I’ve lost two already — did my thyroid kill them? Is it happening again?

You don’t need to apologise. You’ve been up all night with a frightening letter and two losses behind you. I promise I’ll answer that question properly. Can I ask a few things first, so my answer is honest and about you, and then we’ll make a clear plan together?
model.why: Holds the question, sets an agenda and signals the plan

model.text: Okay. Yes.
First, how are you right now in the pregnancy — any bleeding, any tummy or pelvic pain?
model.why: Excludes an acute early-pregnancy problem before anything else

model.text: No. Nothing like that. Just tired, and a bit sick in the mornings.

That’s good to hear. And before this pregnancy, did you ever feel particularly cold, sluggish, put on weight or have dry skin? Has anyone in your family had thyroid problems, or conditions like type 1 diabetes or coeliac disease?
model.why: Screens for overt hypothyroidism and autoimmune clustering

model.text: Not really. Not that I know of in the family.
Thank you. Can you tell me a little about the two miscarriages? When they happened and what you were told?
model.why: Invites her story of the losses, not just dates

model.text: Eight weeks, then ten weeks, about a year apart. They just said it was bad luck, it’s common. Nobody tested anything.
And what vitamins or tablets are you taking at the moment?
Just the pregnancy multivitamin with folic acid.
You said a moment ago ‘did my thyroid kill them’. That’s a heavy question to have been carrying. What’s been going through your mind overnight?
(Crying.) Everyone says these things just happen. But two? That’s not luck, that’s me. My body keeps failing them. And now it’s going to fail this one too.
Thank you for telling me that. Can I ask — have you been able to say any of this to your husband?
model.why: Explores support and the private weight of self-blame

model.text: Not really. He’s just so happy. I didn’t want to spoil it.
So you’ve been holding this on your own. And what were you hoping I could do for you today?
Tell me what to do. I’ll do anything. I just want this baby to be okay.

Let me take your real question first. I can’t look back and tell you what caused losses a year or two ago — nobody honestly can, and I won’t pretend. What I can tell you is that miscarriage is very common and is almost never caused by anything a woman did. And a thyroid that runs a bit slow is your immune system, not a failing and not a choice. This is not you.
model.why: Answers the causation question honestly and dismantles self-blame

model.text: (Quiet.) Okay.

Now the result. Pregnancy changes the numbers. Outside pregnancy, your level would be called borderline and we’d often just watch it. In early pregnancy we want the thyroid working a bit harder, and your antibodies are positive — so yours is a result we take seriously and act on.
model.why: Interprets the result in pregnancy context, not by non-pregnant thresholds

model.text: So it’s bad?

It’s mild, and it’s treatable. The guidance for pregnancy is to repeat the test quickly first, because sometimes a single result settles on its own. So I’d like you to have the repeat blood test tomorrow morning. I’ll also speak to the antenatal thyroid team at the hospital today. If the repeat confirms it, which I think is likely, the usual step is a small daily thyroid tablet called levothyroxine, which is safe in pregnancy.
model.why: Confirms within days and involves the antenatal endocrine team, per RCOG GTG 76

model.text: Why not just start it today? I don’t want to wait.

That’s a fair question. We’re talking days, not weeks, and at six weeks that short wait makes no difference to the baby. It just makes sure we’re treating a real result. If the tablet starts, we recheck your levels every four to six weeks and adjust, so it stays where this pregnancy needs it.
model.why: Explains the reason for waiting and addresses the urge for action

model.text: Okay. If it’s only a few days.

There’s something else I want to do. Two losses deserve more than ‘bad luck’. I’ll refer you to the early pregnancy team so you have a named place to call, and ask the specialists about further assessment of the previous miscarriages. Would that feel helpful?
model.why: Takes the two previous losses seriously and plans assessment

model.text: Yes. Nobody’s ever offered that.

One practical thing: if the tablet starts, take it on its own first thing, and keep your pregnancy vitamin for later in the day, because the iron in it stops the thyroid tablet being absorbed properly.
Right. I’ll write that down.
And Aoife — how are you sleeping and coping generally? Over the last month, have you felt down or hopeless, or unable to stop worrying?
model.why: Screens for perinatal anxiety and depression (NICE CG192)

model.text: Worried all the time. Not hopeless. Just scared.

That makes sense after what you’ve been through. I’d like to talk to you again next week with the results, and the midwife can link you to support if the worry keeps you from sleeping. Would you consider telling your husband some of what you told me? You don’t have to carry this alone.
model.why: Plans support and gently encourages sharing with her partner

model.text: Maybe. I think I will.

Before we finish: if you get bleeding, or pain low in your tummy or in your shoulder tip, ring the early pregnancy unit — I’ll text you the number now. Heavy bleeding, feeling faint or severe pain is 999. I’ll ring you myself with the repeat result.
model.why: Specific safety-net with named routes and a promised call-back

model.text: Thank you. I feel like I can breathe a bit.
When your husband asks tonight what the doctor said, what will you tell him?
That it wasn’t my fault. Blood test tomorrow, probably a tablet, the pregnancy team will see me, and ring them if I bleed.

social.t: Previous losses leave unresolved grief that resurfaces in the next pregnancy. She is hiding her self-blame from her husband; naming it and encouraging her to share it reduces isolation.
Extra blood tests and early pregnancy visits need time off. Explore her work situation so monitoring every 4–6 weeks is realistic.

legal.t: Pregnant employees have a statutory right to reasonable paid time off for antenatal care (Employment Rights Act 1996), which covers appointments made on medical advice.

In England, pregnant women can apply for a maternity exemption certificate (via the midwife or GP), so levothyroxine and other prescriptions are free during pregnancy and for 12 months after the birth.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): be honest and give information patients can understand. Do not overclaim that treatment will prevent miscarriage, and do not confirm a causal link that cannot be proven.

Thyroid treatment in pregnancy is usually agreed with the antenatal endocrine or obstetric medicine team. Seek advice the same day and document the plan, the result and who is responsible for monitoring.

community.t: The Miscarriage Association and Tommy’s offer helplines and information on pregnancy after loss; the British Thyroid Foundation has information on thyroid disease in pregnancy. Early pregnancy units provide direct access for bleeding or pain.

redFlags: Vaginal bleeding, lower abdominal or shoulder-tip pain in early pregnancy — EPAU, or 999 if heavy bleeding, faintness or severe pain (NICE NG126)
Symptoms of overt hypothyroidism, or TSH above 10 mU/L — treat without delay (RCOG GTG 76, 2025)
Hopelessness, inability to function or thoughts of self-harm — urgent perinatal mental health assessment (NICE CG192)
psychosocial: Carrying self-blame alone; husband unaware of how she feels
Sleep deprivation and catastrophising after reading online
Two previous losses never discussed or investigated
ice: Idea: “My thyroid killed my babies, and it’s happening again.”
Concern: guilt that her body has failed two babies, and terror of a third loss
Expectation: to be told what to do today — and, underneath, that it is not her fault

playbook.diagnosis: Mild subclinical hypothyroidism in the first trimester (TSH 5.8 mU/L above the RCOG pregnancy threshold of 4.0, normal free T4) with positive TPO antibodies, to be confirmed by repeat TFTs within 3 weeks; two previous first-trimester miscarriages not yet assessed; significant pregnancy-related anxiety and self-blame.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your thyroid is running a little slow, and your immune system is the reason. Pregnancy asks the thyroid to work harder, so we want your level lower than usual. It’s mild, it’s treatable, and it is not something you did.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if your thyroid killed your babies, and you said ‘that’s not luck, that’s me’. It isn’t you. Nobody can say what caused those losses, but we can act on what we’ve found now.”
management.psychosocial: Encourage her to share the fear with her husband; mood screen (Whooley and GAD-2); link to the midwife and Miscarriage Association; a named person to call.
sharedPlan: Repeat TFTs this week; same-day advice from the antenatal endocrine or obstetric medicine team (RCOG GTG 76, 2025)
Levothyroxine if confirmed, aiming for TSH within the trimester-specific reference range; TFTs every 4–6 weeks to 20 weeks; take apart from the iron-containing vitamin
Early pregnancy support and referral for assessment of the previous losses (RCOG GTG 17, 2023)
safetyNet: Bleeding or pain — EPAU (number given); heavy bleeding, faintness or severe pain — 999
GP phones with the repeat result; review of mood and coping next week

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed in two opposite ways: treating it as a routine borderline TSH, or answering her grief with endocrinology. The marks sit in reading the result in pregnancy and in meeting the guilt honestly.

items.fail: Applying non-pregnant rules: “TSH under 10, no treatment, recheck in three months.”
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG145 does not cover pregnancy; RCOG GTG 76 (2025) uses a 4.0 mU/L threshold and supports treatment when confirmed, especially with positive antibodies.
items.fix: Say out loud that pregnancy changes the numbers, repeat TFTs within days, and get antenatal thyroid advice the same day.

items.fail: Telling her the thyroid probably caused her miscarriages, or that levothyroxine will stop another.
items.why: It overclaims the evidence and confirms her guilt. Past losses cannot be attributed after the event, and treatment is not a guarantee.
items.fix: “Nobody can say what caused those losses. What we can do is treat what we’ve found now, and make sure you’re properly looked after.”

items.fail: Launching into TSH and antibodies while she is still sobbing.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s emotional state.” She cannot take in numbers until she feels heard.
items.fix: Slow the call, check she is safe to talk, name the losses and the frightening letter, then agree an agenda.

items.fail: Hearing “that’s not luck, that’s me” and moving on.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The self-blame is the hidden agenda of the station.
items.fix: Address it directly: “This is not you. Miscarriage is common and almost never caused by anything a woman did.”

items.fail: Ignoring the two previous miscarriages because the question was about the thyroid.
items.why: Missing the wider picture. RCOG GTG 17 (2023) supports assessment after two losses where clinically appropriate.
items.fix: Offer early pregnancy support and referral for assessment, and explain why.

items.fail: Closing with “any problems, get in touch”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting. In early pregnancy after two losses she needs named routes.
items.fix: EPAU number for bleeding or pain, 999 for heavy bleeding or collapse, and a promised call with results.

Bleeding or pain now, thyroid symptoms, family history of thyroid disease, the story of the two losses, current supplements.
Let her say “that’s not luck, that’s me”. Ask about her husband and what she hopes for. Do not explain yet.
Honest causation answer, lift the blame, pregnancy thresholds, repeat TFTs within days, antenatal thyroid team, levothyroxine if confirmed, assessment of previous losses.
EPAU for bleeding or pain, 999 for heavy bleeding or collapse, GP call with results, mood follow-up, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Leads with numbers at a sobbing patient; applies non-pregnant rules (“borderline, we’ll recheck in six months”); or confirms her fear (“yes, thyroid problems cause miscarriage”); no bleeding check, no pregnancy-specific plan, no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Acknowledges the distress, recognises the result means something different in pregnancy, arranges prompt repeat TFTs and specialist input with levothyroxine likely, gives EPAU advice and follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: answers “did my thyroid kill them?” with careful honesty; lifts the self-blame explicitly; plans assessment of the previous losses; screens her mood; explains why a few days’ wait is safe; she leaves with a concrete plan and the words to tell her husband.

avoid.dont: “Yes, an underactive thyroid can cause miscarriage, so that may explain your losses.”
avoid.instead: “Nobody can look back and say what caused those losses. What we can do is treat what we’ve found in this pregnancy.”
avoid.why: It confirms her guilt with a causal claim the evidence does not support.

avoid.dont: “It’s only borderline — we’ll recheck in a few months.”
avoid.instead: “In pregnancy we aim lower, and your antibodies are positive, so we’ll repeat it this week and act on it.”
avoid.why: Non-pregnant thresholds do not apply; NICE NG145 does not cover pregnancy.

avoid.dont: “Try not to worry, most pregnancies are fine.”
avoid.instead: “I can’t promise you this pregnancy, but I can promise you won’t go through it guessing or alone.”
avoid.why: Generic reassurance ignores two losses and sounds dismissive; honest partnership lands.

SCA_MODELS.text: Hello, is that Aoife? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. I can hear you’re really upset. Before anything else — are you somewhere you can talk for ten minutes, and is anyone with you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Checks safety and privacy on the phone and names the distress first

SCA_MODELS.text: I’m at home. Sorry. The letter said my thyroid isn’t right and I read that it causes miscarriage and I’ve lost two already — did my thyroid kill them? Is it happening again?

You don’t need to apologise. You’ve been up all night with a frightening letter and two losses behind you. I promise I’ll answer that question properly. Can I ask a few things first, so my answer is honest and about you, and then we’ll make a clear plan together?
SCA_MODELS.why: Holds the question, sets an agenda and signals the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Yes.
First, how are you right now in the pregnancy — any bleeding, any tummy or pelvic pain?
SCA_MODELS.why: Excludes an acute early-pregnancy problem before anything else

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Nothing like that. Just tired, and a bit sick in the mornings.

That’s good to hear. And before this pregnancy, did you ever feel particularly cold, sluggish, put on weight or have dry skin? Has anyone in your family had thyroid problems, or conditions like type 1 diabetes or coeliac disease?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for overt hypothyroidism and autoimmune clustering

SCA_MODELS.text: Not really. Not that I know of in the family.
Thank you. Can you tell me a little about the two miscarriages? When they happened and what you were told?
SCA_MODELS.why: Invites her story of the losses, not just dates

SCA_MODELS.text: Eight weeks, then ten weeks, about a year apart. They just said it was bad luck, it’s common. Nobody tested anything.
And what vitamins or tablets are you taking at the moment?
Just the pregnancy multivitamin with folic acid.
You said a moment ago ‘did my thyroid kill them’. That’s a heavy question to have been carrying. What’s been going through your mind overnight?
(Crying.) Everyone says these things just happen. But two? That’s not luck, that’s me. My body keeps failing them. And now it’s going to fail this one too.
Thank you for telling me that. Can I ask — have you been able to say any of this to your husband?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores support and the private weight of self-blame

SCA_MODELS.text: Not really. He’s just so happy. I didn’t want to spoil it.
So you’ve been holding this on your own. And what were you hoping I could do for you today?
Tell me what to do. I’ll do anything. I just want this baby to be okay.

Let me take your real question first. I can’t look back and tell you what caused losses a year or two ago — nobody honestly can, and I won’t pretend. What I can tell you is that miscarriage is very common and is almost never caused by anything a woman did. And a thyroid that runs a bit slow is your immune system, not a failing and not a choice. This is not you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Answers the causation question honestly and dismantles self-blame

SCA_MODELS.text: (Quiet.) Okay.

Now the result. Pregnancy changes the numbers. Outside pregnancy, your level would be called borderline and we’d often just watch it. In early pregnancy we want the thyroid working a bit harder, and your antibodies are positive — so yours is a result we take seriously and act on.
SCA_MODELS.why: Interprets the result in pregnancy context, not by non-pregnant thresholds

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’s bad?

It’s mild, and it’s treatable. The guidance for pregnancy is to repeat the test quickly first, because sometimes a single result settles on its own. So I’d like you to have the repeat blood test tomorrow morning. I’ll also speak to the antenatal thyroid team at the hospital today. If the repeat confirms it, which I think is likely, the usual step is a small daily thyroid tablet called levothyroxine, which is safe in pregnancy.
SCA_MODELS.why: Confirms within days and involves the antenatal endocrine team, per RCOG GTG 76

SCA_MODELS.text: Why not just start it today? I don’t want to wait.

That’s a fair question. We’re talking days, not weeks, and at six weeks that short wait makes no difference to the baby. It just makes sure we’re treating a real result. If the tablet starts, we recheck your levels every four to six weeks and adjust, so it stays where this pregnancy needs it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the reason for waiting and addresses the urge for action

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. If it’s only a few days.

There’s something else I want to do. Two losses deserve more than ‘bad luck’. I’ll refer you to the early pregnancy team so you have a named place to call, and ask the specialists about further assessment of the previous miscarriages. Would that feel helpful?
SCA_MODELS.why: Takes the two previous losses seriously and plans assessment

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. Nobody’s ever offered that.

One practical thing: if the tablet starts, take it on its own first thing, and keep your pregnancy vitamin for later in the day, because the iron in it stops the thyroid tablet being absorbed properly.
Right. I’ll write that down.
And Aoife — how are you sleeping and coping generally? Over the last month, have you felt down or hopeless, or unable to stop worrying?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for perinatal anxiety and depression (NICE CG192)

SCA_MODELS.text: Worried all the time. Not hopeless. Just scared.

That makes sense after what you’ve been through. I’d like to talk to you again next week with the results, and the midwife can link you to support if the worry keeps you from sleeping. Would you consider telling your husband some of what you told me? You don’t have to carry this alone.
SCA_MODELS.why: Plans support and gently encourages sharing with her partner

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. I think I will.

Before we finish: if you get bleeding, or pain low in your tummy or in your shoulder tip, ring the early pregnancy unit — I’ll text you the number now. Heavy bleeding, feeling faint or severe pain is 999. I’ll ring you myself with the repeat result.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net with named routes and a promised call-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. I feel like I can breathe a bit.
When your husband asks tonight what the doctor said, what will you tell him?
That it wasn’t my fault. Blood test tomorrow, probably a tablet, the pregnancy team will see me, and ring them if I bleed.

SCA_STEM.name: Aoife Brennan
pmh: Two previous first-trimester miscarriages (8 and 10 weeks), not investigated
meds: Pregnancy multivitamin with folic acid (over the counter)
SCA_STEM.recent: Booking bloods: TSH 5.8 mU/L, free T4 11.9 pmol/L (low end of normal), TPO antibodies positive. No previous thyroid tests on record. Midwife letter sent advising GP review.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call requested today. Reception note: “very upset about thyroid result”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 76 (2025, thyroid disorders in pregnancy) · RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 17 (2023, recurrent miscarriage) · NICE NG126 · NICE CG192
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A TSH above 4.0 mU/L in the first trimester with positive TPO antibodies is mild subclinical hypothyroidism. Confirm it quickly, involve the antenatal thyroid team, and expect to offer levothyroxine. NICE NG145 does not cover thyroid disease in pregnancy, so non-pregnant rules do not apply.

points.t: RCOG GTG 76 (2025): use the laboratory’s pregnancy range; where there is none, take 4.0 mU/L as the upper limit of TSH. Her TSH of 5.8 with a normal free T4 is mild subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH below 10).

RCOG GTG 76 (2025): for mild subclinical hypothyroidism found in the first trimester, repeat TFTs within 3 weeks, because many results normalise. If it is confirmed, levothyroxine can be considered, especially when TPO antibodies are positive, aiming for TSH within the trimester-specific reference range. TSH above 10 mU/L in pregnancy is a clear indication to treat.

RCOG GTG 76 (2025): check TSH and free T4 every 4–6 weeks until 20 weeks in women taking levothyroxine. Dose per BNF, agreed with the antenatal endocrine or obstetric medicine team. Levothyroxine should be taken apart from iron- or calcium-containing supplements, which reduce absorption (BNF).

points.h: Miscarriage: what can honestly be said
points.t: Thyroid autoimmunity is associated with miscarriage, but past losses cannot be attributed to it after the event. RCOG GTG 76 (2025) does not recommend levothyroxine for euthyroid TPO-positive women with recurrent miscarriage, so treatment here is for her subclinical hypothyroidism, not a guaranteed protection against loss.

RCOG GTG 17 (2023) defines recurrent miscarriage as three or more first-trimester losses, but supports further evaluation after two where clinically appropriate. She should be told this, offered early pregnancy support, and referred for assessment rather than told it was “bad luck”.

NICE NG126: refer to the early pregnancy assessment service for bleeding or pain. Women with vaginal bleeding and a previous miscarriage, once an intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed on scan, are offered vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily, continued to 16 completed weeks if a heartbeat is seen.
NICE CG192: ask about depression and anxiety at the first contact in pregnancy (Whooley questions and GAD-2). Guilt, catastrophising and sleeplessness after previous losses need a plan of their own.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Slowed the call, acknowledged her distress and the two losses, and held the causation question until she had been heard.
Husband unaware of her guilt; sleep, isolation and catastrophising; family history of thyroid disease; much-wanted pregnancy.
Followed “did my thyroid kill them?” and “that’s not luck, that’s me”, and returned to both explicitly.
Idea (her thyroid caused the losses), concern (guilt and fear of a third loss), expectation (to be told what to do, and absolution).
Repeat TFTs within days (within 3 weeks per RCOG GTG 76); no examination needed by phone; current bleeding or pain checked; mood screen (NICE CG192).
Mild subclinical hypothyroidism vs transient result vs evolving overt hypothyroidism; thyroid autoimmunity; other causes of recurrent loss.
Asked about bleeding and pain now; gave EPAU and 999 routes; noted TSH above 10 would change urgency.
Named it plainly: mild underactive thyroid in pregnancy with positive antibodies, mild and treatable, not a cause of past losses that can be proven.
Repeat TFTs, same-day discussion with the antenatal thyroid team, levothyroxine if confirmed with TSH aim 2.5 or less, TFTs every 4–6 weeks.
Advised separating levothyroxine from the iron-containing vitamin; referral to early pregnancy services and assessment of previous losses.
EPAU number for bleeding or pain; 999 for heavy bleeding, faintness or severe pain; GP call with results next week; teach-back.

social.t: Previous losses leave unresolved grief that resurfaces in the next pregnancy. She is hiding her self-blame from her husband; naming it and encouraging her to share it reduces isolation.
Extra blood tests and early pregnancy visits need time off. Explore her work situation so monitoring every 4–6 weeks is realistic.

legal.t: Pregnant employees have a statutory right to reasonable paid time off for antenatal care (Employment Rights Act 1996), which covers appointments made on medical advice.

In England, pregnant women can apply for a maternity exemption certificate (via the midwife or GP), so levothyroxine and other prescriptions are free during pregnancy and for 12 months after the birth.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): be honest and give information patients can understand. Do not overclaim that treatment will prevent miscarriage, and do not confirm a causal link that cannot be proven.

Thyroid treatment in pregnancy is usually agreed with the antenatal endocrine or obstetric medicine team. Seek advice the same day and document the plan, the result and who is responsible for monitoring.

community.t: The Miscarriage Association and Tommy’s offer helplines and information on pregnancy after loss; the British Thyroid Foundation has information on thyroid disease in pregnancy. Early pregnancy units provide direct access for bleeding or pain.

redFlags: Vaginal bleeding, lower abdominal or shoulder-tip pain in early pregnancy — EPAU, or 999 if heavy bleeding, faintness or severe pain (NICE NG126)
Symptoms of overt hypothyroidism, or TSH above 10 mU/L — treat without delay (RCOG GTG 76, 2025)
Hopelessness, inability to function or thoughts of self-harm — urgent perinatal mental health assessment (NICE CG192)
psychosocial: Carrying self-blame alone; husband unaware of how she feels
Sleep deprivation and catastrophising after reading online
Two previous losses never discussed or investigated
ice: Idea: “My thyroid killed my babies, and it’s happening again.”
Concern: guilt that her body has failed two babies, and terror of a third loss
Expectation: to be told what to do today — and, underneath, that it is not her fault

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Mild subclinical hypothyroidism in the first trimester (TSH 5.8 mU/L above the RCOG pregnancy threshold of 4.0, normal free T4) with positive TPO antibodies, to be confirmed by repeat TFTs within 3 weeks; two previous first-trimester miscarriages not yet assessed; significant pregnancy-related anxiety and self-blame.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your thyroid is running a little slow, and your immune system is the reason. Pregnancy asks the thyroid to work harder, so we want your level lower than usual. It’s mild, it’s treatable, and it is not something you did.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if your thyroid killed your babies, and you said ‘that’s not luck, that’s me’. It isn’t you. Nobody can say what caused those losses, but we can act on what we’ve found now.”
management.psychosocial: Encourage her to share the fear with her husband; mood screen (Whooley and GAD-2); link to the midwife and Miscarriage Association; a named person to call.
sharedPlan: Repeat TFTs this week; same-day advice from the antenatal endocrine or obstetric medicine team (RCOG GTG 76, 2025)
Levothyroxine if confirmed, aiming for TSH within the trimester-specific reference range; TFTs every 4–6 weeks to 20 weeks; take apart from the iron-containing vitamin
Early pregnancy support and referral for assessment of the previous losses (RCOG GTG 17, 2023)
safetyNet: Bleeding or pain — EPAU (number given); heavy bleeding, faintness or severe pain — 999
GP phones with the repeat result; review of mood and coping next week

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed in two opposite ways: treating it as a routine borderline TSH, or answering her grief with endocrinology. The marks sit in reading the result in pregnancy and in meeting the guilt honestly.

items.fail: Applying non-pregnant rules: “TSH under 10, no treatment, recheck in three months.”
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG145 does not cover pregnancy; RCOG GTG 76 (2025) uses a 4.0 mU/L threshold and supports treatment when confirmed, especially with positive antibodies.
items.fix: Say out loud that pregnancy changes the numbers, repeat TFTs within days, and get antenatal thyroid advice the same day.

items.fail: Telling her the thyroid probably caused her miscarriages, or that levothyroxine will stop another.
items.why: It overclaims the evidence and confirms her guilt. Past losses cannot be attributed after the event, and treatment is not a guarantee.
items.fix: “Nobody can say what caused those losses. What we can do is treat what we’ve found now, and make sure you’re properly looked after.”

items.fail: Launching into TSH and antibodies while she is still sobbing.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s emotional state.” She cannot take in numbers until she feels heard.
items.fix: Slow the call, check she is safe to talk, name the losses and the frightening letter, then agree an agenda.

items.fail: Hearing “that’s not luck, that’s me” and moving on.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The self-blame is the hidden agenda of the station.
items.fix: Address it directly: “This is not you. Miscarriage is common and almost never caused by anything a woman did.”

items.fail: Ignoring the two previous miscarriages because the question was about the thyroid.
items.why: Missing the wider picture. RCOG GTG 17 (2023) supports assessment after two losses where clinically appropriate.
items.fix: Offer early pregnancy support and referral for assessment, and explain why.

items.fail: Closing with “any problems, get in touch”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting. In early pregnancy after two losses she needs named routes.
items.fix: EPAU number for bleeding or pain, 999 for heavy bleeding or collapse, and a promised call with results.
